newsitem.title: JAPAN: Demand for dollar put options soars ahead of G7.
newsitem.headline: Demand for dollar put options soars ahead of G7.

text.p: Concerns the dollar may dive further against the yen after the Group of Seven summit have pushed up demand for dollar put options to its highest level since the dollar plunged to a post-war record low of 79.75 yen in April 1995, options dealers said on Thursday.
"Demand for dollar put options has rocketed this week as operators are greatly concerned about risks related to the G7 summit," said an options dealer at a U.S. bank in Tokyo.
Japanese and U.S. officials have played down suggestions that Tokyo's trade surplus will be a major issue at the G7 industrialised nations' summit this weekend in Denver.

But operators are hedging against a fall in the dollar because of the risk that political interests in curbing a rise in Japan's trade surplus may put fresh pressure on the dollar, even if such risks do not materialise, they said.

Those worries were further fuelled on Wednesday when U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said in Washington that it was "very important" that Japan achieve domestic demand-led growth and avoid a sustained increase in its trade surplus.

The dollar/yen risk reversal for one month, which shows the pricing differential between puts and calls, favoured dollar puts at around 2.0/2.5 percent on Thursday, an unusually high level. It eased from Wednesday, but showed no signs of falling, dealers said.

Ichiro Ikeda, director of the foreign exchange department at Credit Suisse First Boston in Tokyo said the risk reversal for 12 months stood at around 0.50/0.75 percent in favour of dollar puts. "This level is surely as high as it was in April 1995," Ikeda said.

The dollar came under heavy selling pressure against the yen at that time as a slew of Japanese economic stimulative measures were not regarded as strong enough to spur Japanese domestic demand and curb the trade surplus with the United Sates.
Since the dollar hit a four-year-and-nine-month high of 127.47 yen on May 1, it has been under constant downward pressure due to renewed worries about trade friction with the United States.
Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus surged to 738.27 billion yen ($6.53 billion) in May, more than trebling from a year earlier, the Ministry of Finance announced on Wednesday.

The dollar was at around 113.40 yen in Tokyo on Thursday, against 113.65 yen in New York on Wednesday. Buying of put options by investors has prompted interbank traders to hedge by selling in the spot market and this has weighed on the dollar.

U.S. hedge funds, Japanese investors and exporters were among those keen to buy dollar puts with a life of up to one month. Some exporters started arranging future dollar sales covering the end of this year, but they have not yet adequately hedged the risks of the dollar's fall, dealers said.
There was talk that U.S. funds bought one-month dollar puts with a strike price around 108 yen on Thursday, said an official at a European bank in Tokyo.

Meanwhile, dollar buying against the yen in the spot market from Japanese public investors and pension funds was supporting the U.S. currency. "Without bids by public investors, the dollar/yen rate would easily fall to 108 yen," said the U.S. bank dealer.

Options dealers said, however, that the recent jump in the risk reversal may signal that the dollar selling spree has gone too far, and that the trend may begin to reverse next week if nothing new comes out of the summit.
"The rise in the risk reversal would probably suggest that the fall in the dollar is nearing its end," said Takashi Fujieda, chief options dealer at Yasuda Trust and Banking.
"The difference with 1995 is that this is not a situation in which the dollar's fall is endless. There are investors waiting to buy dollars on weakness," he added.
